The American Falls at Niagara Falls turned off for inspection and repair. New York. 1969

For six months in the summer and fall of 1969, Niagara’s American Falls were “de-watered”, as the Army Corps of Engineers conducted a geological survey of the Falls face and cleared rock from the base. Rockslides had caused a significant buildup of rock at the bottom of the falls and the engineers were to clean up the rock and repair some faults to prevent eventual erosion of the American side of the waterfall.

A temporary dam was built to divert the flow of water to the Canadian side's Horseshoe Falls. The dam measured 600 feet (180 m) across and was made of nearly 30,000 tons of rock. In this picture you can see the dam.

The engineers cleared the rock debris and tested for safety, finishing the project in November of that year. Water flow was restored on November 25, 1969.

Source.
Explains why those big slabs of rock look so "new". You'd think all the rocks at the bottom of the falls would be more worn away.

Throughout the geologic record, those rocks are refreshed. The water going over the edge of the cliff, forming the waterfall, causes erosion of the cliff face. As more erosion happens, more rocks are calved off and tumble down into the river. The water will also wear them down and send them down the river, over time.

The Niagara River flows from Lake Eire to Lake Ontario. Over thousands of years, the falls have moved upstream through this erosion process about 6-7 miles.

It doesn't happen fast, but the wearing down of the rocks at the bottom of the falls doesn't happen fast either. So, basically, the rocks at the bottom of the falls are new, relatively speaking.
